title: Star, moon, sun
hookLine: the young Ibrahim watches a star, the moon, the sun set, and says he will not love what sets (6:76–79)

cards: Lie on your back somewhere dark, far from the city. The first star comes out, so bright you'd swear it was a plane. Later the moon rises, huge and orange, and the star looks small.
In the morning the sun swallows them both. By evening, the sun is gone too. Long ago, a young man watched that same sky and asked a question.
His name was Ibrahim, Abraham, a prophet honored by Jews, Christians and Muslims alike.

teach.b: Surah six. Ibrahim lives among people who worship idols and the lights of the sky. Night falls, and he sees a star.
This is my Lord, he says. Then the star sets, and he says, in Pickthall's words: “I love not things that set.”

teach.h: THE MOON, THE SUN: GONE TOO.
teach.b: The moon rises, brighter: this is my Lord. The moon sets. Then the sun, blazing: this is my Lord, this one is greater.
And the sun goes down too. So he turns away from all of it, toward the One who made the heavens and the earth, as one by nature upright.
The Arabic word is hanif: the one who leans toward God, and away from everything else. Scholars read this scene two ways, and both are old.
Some say it's a young man truly searching, trying each light in turn, until he sees that anything that disappears can't be God.

Others point to the verses around it. His people worshipped the stars, and Ibrahim, they say, already knew. He was walking them through their own logic out loud, star by star, so they could hear where it led.
Either way, his test is simple enough for a child. Does it set? Does it fade, or leave, or go dark?
Then it can't be the thing you give your whole heart to.

teach.h: I LOVE NOT THINGS THAT SET.
teach.b: His word for things that set, afilin, also means things that fade and vanish. It's a question you can ask of almost anything you love too much.

how: Muslims call Ibrahim hanif, upright, and the model of pure faith; the Qur'an tells Muslims to follow the religion of Ibrahim, and a blessing recited near the end of the prayer names him.

o: the sign Ibrahim's people said would never fade
a light that guided Ibrahim's family on their journey
the first light Ibrahim saw set, before the moon and sun

games.q: what's inside the scene — tap the pairs.
p: this one is greater — and it set too
things that set, fade and vanish

s: scholars agree Ibrahim was truly worshipping the star
some say he was searching; others that he was walking his people through their own logic.
Ibrahim's test was whether a thing sets
Jews, Christians and Muslims each honor Ibrahim
Abraham, Ibrahim: honored in all three.

games.q: you've watched the star set, then the moon, then even the sun. what do you conclude?
o: the brightest light must be God.
none of what sets is God; turn to the One who made them.
there's nothing up there at all.
games.why: he turned his face to the One who created the heavens and the earth, as a hanif, upright.

practice: If you can, look out a window at the sky, day or night; if not, picture the last sky you saw. Watch the light for a few slow breaths, and notice that even up there, things are moving.
If you pray, turn your face, as Ibrahim did, toward the One who made it all.

wordCard.voice: Star. The first light Ibrahim saw set, then the moon, then the sun, and he said: I love not things that set.

orig.note: Arabic: "I love not things that set" (6:76); afilin are things that sink, fade and vanish.

carryVoice: Your line: love what doesn't set. Ibrahim's whole test fits in three words: does it set? See you tomorrow.

sources.q: I love not things that set.

sources.ref: Qur'an 6:74–79, 83 (the star, the moon, the sun; turning the face; the argument given to Ibrahim)
